lesson.title: No Article? The Adjective Goes Strong
lesson.subtitle: kaltes Wasser, heißer Tee, guter Wein — the adjective does the article's job alone

hook.title: The Adjective Promoted to Flag-Carrier
hook.content: Last lesson's law: one flag-carrier per noun phrase. der shows the case, the adjective whispers -e — der kalte Tag. But German nouns often roam FREE — no article at all: Kaltes Wasser ist gut. Heißer Tee, bitte. The moment the article steps out, the adjective is promoted: it must do the article's job alone, wearing the full strong ending — -er for masculine, -es for neuter, -e for feminine. This is the oldest layer of the system, and English once wore it too: Old English said gōd mann (strong, no article) but se gōda mann (weak, after the). English dropped both sets of endings; German kept them both, working.

footnotes.title: Strong and Weak, the Old English Way
footnotes.content: Linguists call the no-article endings the STRONG declension and the der/die/das endings the WEAK declension — the same terms used for Old English grammar (strong gōd mann vs weak se gōda mann). The names describe which word carries the case-flag: alone (strong) or propped up by a flagged article (weak).

pattern.title: The Strong Endings Are the Demonstrative Endings
pattern.content: Watch the pattern: the strong adjective borrows the endings of der/die/das itself — guter Wein (masculine -er, like der), kaltes Wasser (neuter -es, like das), gute Butter (feminine -e, like die). The article-less noun phrase is its own little demonstrative. Mixed recap: ein hides its flag in the masculine nominative (ein guter Wein) and neuter (ein kaltes Wasser) — the adjective covers for it — but einen, eine, einer carry their own flags, so the adjective falls back to weak: einen besseren Kaffee (the very form the capstone whispered). And in the no-article plural the adjective takes -e: alte Bücher, alte Wörter.
pattern.linguist_note: The strong endings are the old demonstrative pronoun endings (*sa, *sō, *þat) — German spread them onto the adjective so that even a bare noun phrase still announces case and gender. English kept the pronouns (he, she, that) but let the adjective go naked.

exercises.prompt: Bare-noun phrases (no article!) — match each with its reading. Then recall earlier vocabulary in the short phrases:
exercises.target_answer: kaltes Wasser, heißer Tee, guter Wein, altes Brot, Die Straße ist lang, Das Brot ist lecker
exercises.meaning: cold water (no article); hot tea (no article); good wine (no article); old bread (no article); The street is long; The bread is tasty
exercises.explanation: No article → the adjective goes strong: -es after neuter nouns, -er after masculine, mirroring der/das themselves. But predicates rest bare: der Zug ist schnell, der Kuchen ist lecker und schwer, alles ist neu, der Kühlschrank ist voll, die Straße ist nass — no endings when nothing follows the adjective.

exercises.prompt: No article, neuter noun: '_____ Wasser ist kalt.' (cold):
exercises.meaning: Kaltes Wasser ist kalt = cold water is cold
exercises.explanation: Neuter strong ending -es — the adjective copies das: kaltes Wasser. It is doing the article's job alone.

exercises.explanation: heißer — the strong masculine -er, borrowed straight from der. Heißer Tee, bitte.

exercises.prompt: The capstone's whisper, decoded: 'Ich trinke einen _____ Kaffee.' (better):
exercises.meaning: einen besseren Kaffee = a better coffee
exercises.explanation: einen already carries the accusative flag, so the adjective goes weak: besseren. The flag passes from article to adjective only when the article goes quiet.

exercises.prompt: Say in German: "Kaltes Wasser ist besser als warmer Kaffee = cold water is better than warm coffee"
exercises.target_answer: Kaltes Wasser ist besser als warmer Kaffee
exercises.meaning: Kaltes Wasser ist besser als warmer Kaffee = cold water is better than warm coffee

vocab_hints.note: strong ending -er after a bare masculine noun

exercises.explanation: Two strong adjectives in one sentence — kaltes (neuter) and warmer (masculine) — plus the als-comparison from the Sentence Gym.
exercises.idea: Kaltes Wasser ist besser als warmer Kaffee = cold water is better than warm coffee
idea_parts: Kaltes Wasser ist besser als warmer Kaffee
= cold water is better than warm coffee (verb in position 2)
cues: Start with "Kaltes" and anchor "Wasser" in position 2.

summary.outcome: Decline adjectives before bare nouns (strong) and after ein-family flags (mixed), including einen besseren Kaffee.

use_example.german: Kaltes Wasser ist besser als warmer Kaffee.
use_example.english: Cold water is better than warm coffee.

summary.takeaway: No article → the adjective goes strong (-er/-es/-e, the demonstrative endings); a flagged article → the adjective falls back to weak.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: hidden shifts I — the quiet V→B family: geben↔give, über↔over, sieben↔seven.

wein.etymology_derivation: Early Latin loanword vinum entered into both Old English and Old High German.

brot.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *braudą — originally "the fermented/risen thing", kin to the verb brew (German brauen). Bread is "the brewed thing". [wiktionary]

warm.etymology_derivation: Identical form and meaning as English warm since Old High German. [wiktionary]

voll.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fullaz — English full is the explicit cognate. [wiktionary]

nass.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *nat — cognate with Dutch nat; English wet is a translation match, not a cognate. [wiktionary]

schnell.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German snel, Proto-Germanic *snellaz, meaning quick and bold; the exact English cognate is the rare word snell, still heard in northern England and Scotland. [wiktionary]

schwer.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *swēraz 'heavy, grave'; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

lecker.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German lecker, tied to the verb lecken, to lick, Proto-West Germanic *likkōn; the entry points to English lick as the relative, so the word family is literally about licking. [wiktionary]

neu.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German niuwe, Proto-Germanic *niwjaz, the exact twin of English new; both go back to the same Indo-European root. [wiktionary]
